newsitem.title: LATVIA: Baltics cautiously welcome summit outcome.
newsitem.headline: Baltics cautiously welcome summit outcome.

text.p: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania cautiously welcomed the outcome of the Helsinki summit, saying it produced no unpleasant surprises.

Russia is particularly sensitive about its western flank and about large Russian minorities in the three former Soviet Baltic republics, which are anxious to secure their independence by joining NATO.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin restated in Helsinki Moscow's firm opposition to the eastward expansion of NATO but U.S. President Bill Clinton said that Western alliance would expand as planned.
"From my point of view, the situation could not have got any more positive, but it could have got more negative and this did not happen," Latvian Foreign Minister Valdis Birkavs told Reuters.
Some Baltic diplomats had expressed concern ahead of the summit that a secret deal would be cut in Helsinki which would leave their countries stranded on the eastern side of a new iron curtain.
Birkavs said that Latvia welcomed America's resolve to push forward with expansion in the face strong Russian objections.
"The meeting went as expected and the results were as expected," he added.

"The West has reached another milestone in engaging Russia. They have reached an understanding about the nature of the relationship between NATO and Russia," said Mart Laanemae, the deputy under-secretary of the Estonian foreign ministry.
In Lithuania, Foreign Minister Algirdas Saudargas said that at least one Baltic country had to be included in the first round of NATO enlargement.
NATO is expected to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic for accession talks during a summit in Madrid in July.
Diplomats and analysts have all but written the Baltic states off as first-round candidates on the grounds that their inclusion would be regarded as a provocation by Moscow.
"In order to mitigate (Baltic) security concerns, at least one Baltic state should be included in the first wave of NATO expansion," Saudargas said.
"This would be an unambiguous demonstration that the Baltic states are in the stream toward membership," he said.
He added that he was "encouraged that regardless of disagreements NATO enlargement will proceed as scheduled.
